title: The role of artificial intelligence in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals
extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) may influence progress toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Rather than evaluating a single educational intervention, it uses a consensus-based expert elicitation process to map published evidence linking AI to all 17 SDGs and their 169 targets. The central question is whether AI is more often an enabler or inhibitor of sustainable development, and where current research is strong versus weak.

The paper does not study a population of learners, teachers, or schools. Instead, it synthesizes evidence from real-world applications, controlled/laboratory studies, reports from accredited organizations, and documented commercial-stage applications across sectors such as society, economy, and environment. The authors classify evidence by strength and note that many apparent benefits come from studies conducted in controlled environments, with limited generalizability to real-world settings.

The main conclusion is that AI can potentially enable many SDG targets, but it can also hinder others, especially through inequality, bias, energy use, weak transparency, and inadequate oversight. The paper argues that current AI research is biased toward positive outcomes and that stronger regulatory insight, ethical safeguards, and context-sensitive deployment are needed to realize benefits while minimizing harms. For the requested K-12 science comparison-study question, this paper is not a target-domain study and reports none of the educational outcome features of interest (e.g., delayed post-tests, transfer tasks, subgroup effects, or implementation fidelity).
quality_tier_rationale: This is a broad perspective/expert-elicitation paper, not a K-12 causal comparison study of an AI-powered science intervention. It does not report an empirical design, student outcomes, delayed post-tests, transfer tasks, subgroup analyses, or implementation fidelity for any target-domain educational study.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper offers only high-level claims about AI and sustainable development, including education in general, but no measured educational impact. After retaining only true K-12 science causal comparison studies on AI tools for scientific reasoning/inquiry, this paper provides no usable evidence to support the optimistic thesis or any narrower conditional claim.
